claim: Topoisomerase V is a unique topoisomerase that combines DNA repair and topoisomerase activities.
source: Topoisomerase V is a unique topoisomerase that combines DNA repair and topoisomerase activities.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Belova et al., 2001; Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: The enzyme has an unusual arrangement, with a small topoisomerase domain followed by 12 tandem (HhH)2 domains, which include 3 AP lyase repair domains.
source: The enzyme has an unusual arrangement, with a small topoisomerase domain followed by 12 tandem (HhH)2 domains, which include 3 AP lyase repair domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the domain organization. The structure is supported by previous characterization (Belova et al., 2002; Shao and Grishin, 2000; Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013).

claim: The uncommon architecture of topoisomerase V bears no resemblance to any other known topoisomerase.
source: The uncommon architecture of this enzyme bears no resemblance to any other known topoisomerase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Forterre, 2006; Taneja et al., 2006) indicating lack of sequence or structural similarities.

claim: The (HhH)2 domains wrap around the DNA and appear to act as a processivity factor.
source: The structures show that the (HhH)2 domains wrap around the DNA and in this manner appear to act as a processivity factor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in the structures (Figures 1, 2). The interpretation is based on structural observations and comparison with known processivity factors.

claim: There is a conformational change in the protein to expose the topoisomerase active site.
source: There is a conformational change in the protein to expose the topoisomerase active site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, showing the breaking of Linker helix I.

claim: The DNA bends sharply to enter the active site, which melts the DNA and probably facilitates relaxation.
source: The DNA bends sharply to enter the active site, which melts the DNA and probably facilitates relaxation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figures 2D and 3C. The melting is observed in the structure, and the facilitation of relaxation is inferred.

claim: Topoisomerase V relaxes DNA using a controlled rotation mechanism.
source: In common with type IB enzymes, topoisomerase V relaxes DNA using a controlled rotation mechanism, but the structures show that topoisomerase V accomplishes this in different manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous single-molecule experiments (Taneja et al., 2007) cited in the discussion.

claim: Type IC topoisomerases form a distinct type of topoisomerases, with no similarities to other types at the sequence, structural, or mechanistic level.
source: Overall, the structures firmly establish that type IC topoisomerases form a distinct type of topoisomerases, with no similarities to other types at the sequence, structural, or mechanistic level.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the structural data presented and comparison with other topoisomerase types.

claim: Type IC topoisomerases represent a completely different solution to DNA relaxation.
source: They represent a completely different solution to DNA relaxation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the structural and mechanistic findings.

claim: Topoisomerases are found in all three domains of life.
source: Topoisomerases are found in all three domains of life, but the diversity in structure and sequence suggests that the major subtypes evolved independently (Forterre et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Forterre et al., 2007.

claim: All topoisomerases have in common the use of phosphotyrosine intermediates for transient cleavage through a transesterification mechanism.
source: All topoisomerases have in common the use of phosphotyrosine intermediates for transient cleavage through a transesterification mechanism (Corbett and Berger, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Corbett and Berger, 2004.

claim: Topoisomerases are classified into two types (I and II) based on whether they cleave one or two strands of DNA in a concerted manner.
source: Topoisomerases are classified into two types (I and II) based on whether they cleave one or two strands of DNA in a concerted manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Type I enzymes are subclassified into three subtypes, IA, IB, and IC.
source: Type I enzymes, which cleave one DNA strand, are subclassified into three subtypes, IA, IB, and IC.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established classification in the field.

claim: Type IA enzymes employ an enzyme-bridged strand passage mechanism.
source: Type IA enzymes are found in bacteria, archaea, and eukarya, employ an enzyme-bridged strand passage mechanism, and share a strand passage structural domain with a very characteristic toroidal shape (Lima et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Lima et al., 1994.

claim: Type IB enzymes employ a swiveling or controlled rotation mechanism.
source: Type IB enzymes are also found in all domains of life, employ a swiveling or controlled rotation mechanism, and show clear structural and sequence similarities, despite some of them being much larger than other members of the same subtype (Corbett and Berger, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Corbett and Berger, 2004.

claim: Topoisomerases of the third subtype, IC, have only been found in the archaeal Methanopyrus genus.
source: Topoisomerases of the third subtype, IC, have only been found in the archaeal Methanopyrus genus (Forterre, 2006) and relax DNA using a controlled rotation/swiveling mechanism (Taneja et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Forterre, 2006.

claim: Topoisomerase V was originally described as a type IB enzyme but later classified into its own subtype due to the lack of sequence or structural similarities with other topoisomerases.
source: Its only member is topoisomerase V, which was originally described as a type IB enzyme (Slesarev et al., 1993), but later classified into its own subtype due to the lack of sequence or structural similarities with other topoisomerases (Forterre, 2006; Taneja et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Slesarev et al., 1993; Forterre, 2006; Taneja et al., 2006.

claim: Topoisomerase V works at extremely high temperatures (65–122°C) and in high salt concentrations.
source: Topoisomerase V works not only at extremely high temperatures (65–122°C), but also in high salt concentrations (Slesarev et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Slesarev et al., 1994.

claim: Topoisomerase V combines DNA repair and topoisomerization activities in the same polypeptide, a unique feature of this enzyme.
source: It is also an unusual protein as it combines DNA repair and topoisomerization activities in the same polypeptide (Belova et al., 2001; Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013), a unique feature of this enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Belova et al., 2001; Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013.

claim: Topoisomerase V is formed by a small, ~30-kDa topoisomerase domain followed by 24 tandem helix–hairpin–helix (HhH) repeats arranged as 12 (HhH)2 domains.
source: Topoisomerase V is formed by a small, ~30-kDa topoisomerase domain followed by 24 tandem helix–hairpin–helix (HhH) repeats (Doherty et al., 1996) arranged as 12 (HhH)2 domains (Belova et al., 2002; Shao and Grishin, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Doherty et al., 1996; Belova et al., 2002; Shao and Grishin, 2000.

claim: 3 of the 12 (HhH)2 domains have apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) lyase and deoxyribose-5-phosphate (dRP) lyase activities.
source: HhH repeats are associated with DNA lyase repair activity (Doherty et al., 1996; Shao and Grishin, 2000) and 3 of the 12 (HhH)2 domains have apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) lyase and deoxyribose-5-phosphate (dRP) lyase activities (Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013.

claim: The 12 (HhH)2 domains stimulate the topoisomerase activity as mutant topoisomerase V proteins with fewer repeats show decreasing relaxation activity.
source: These 12 (HhH)2 domains also stimulate the topoisomerase activity as mutant topoisomerase V proteins with fewer repeats show decreasing relaxation activity (Belova et al., 2002; Rajan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Belova et al., 2002; Rajan et al., 2010.

claim: (HhH)2 domains are usually found as isolated domains, not in tandem arrangements.
source: (HhH)2 domains are usually found as isolated domains, not in tandem arrangements (Shao and Grishin, 2000), which is another unusual characteristic of topoisomerase V.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Shao and Grishin, 2000.

claim: The topoisomerase domain has no sequence or structural similarities to other topoisomerases or any other protein, making it a unique fold.
source: The topoisomerase domain has no sequence or structural similarities to other topoisomerases or any other protein, making it a unique fold (Forterre, 2006; Taneja et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Forterre, 2006; Taneja et al., 2006.

claim: The active site residues of topoisomerase V have been identified.
source: The active site residues have been identified (Rajan et al., 2014), and their three dimensional arrangement suggests a different catalytic mechanism from other topoisomerases (Rajan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Rajan et al., 2014.

claim: The three dimensional arrangement of active site residues suggests a different catalytic mechanism from other topoisomerases.
source: The active site residues have been identified (Rajan et al., 2014), and their three dimensional arrangement suggests a different catalytic mechanism from other topoisomerases (Rajan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Rajan et al., 2014.

claim: In the structures of the free protein, the topoisomerase domain active site is inaccessible as it is covered by the (HhH)2 domains.
source: In the structures of the free protein, the topoisomerase domain active site is inaccessible as it is covered by the (HhH)2 domains (Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013; Rajan et al., 2010; Taneja et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013; Rajan et al., 2010; Taneja et al., 2006.

claim: Topoisomerase V is a nonsequence-specific DNA-binding protein that has AP lyase activity and interacts with DNA abasic sites.
source: Topoisomerase V is a nonsequence-specific DNA-binding protein that has AP lyase activity and interacts with DNA abasic sites (Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Rajan et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2013.

claim: The optimal crystals grew with a 38-base pair (bp) DNA oligonucleotide with a single abasic site and two complementary overhanging base pairs at the ends of the DNA.
source: After trying several DNA sequences, lengths, and overhangs, the optimal crystals grew with a 38-base pair (bp) DNA oligonucleotide with a single abasic site and two complementary overhanging base pairs at the ends of the DNA (Materials and methods and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing crystallization experiments.

claim: The structure with asymmetric DNA is in a closed conformation.
source: This structure is in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the asymmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The crystals of the complex formed by Topo-97(ΔRS2) with a 38-bp asymmetric DNA oligonucleotide diffract to 3.24 Å in the best direction but only to ~3.9 Å in the other directions.
source: The crystals of the complex formed by Topo-97(ΔRS2) with a 38-bp asymmetric DNA oligonucleotide containing one abasic site diffract to a 3.24 Å in the best direction but only to ~3.9 Å in the other directions (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contains two complexes, each formed by a Topo-97(ΔRS2) protein molecule and two different DNA molecules.
source: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contains two complexes, each formed by a Topo-97(ΔRS2) protein molecule and two different DNA molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each protein monomer is bound to only half of each DNA molecule in the asymmetric complex.
source: This arrangement is unusual, with each protein monomer bound to only half of each DNA molecule.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the asymmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The center of two of the half-bound DNA molecules sits on crystallographic twofold axes, recreating the full-length DNA.
source: The center of two of the half-bound DNA molecules sits on crystallographic twofold axes, recreating the full-length DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two complexes in the asymmetric unit are very similar, but not identical (root mean square deviation [rmsd] between Cα atoms ~1.0 Å).
source: The two complexes in the asymmetric unit are very similar, but not identical (root mean square deviation [rmsd] between Cα atoms ~1.0 Å).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the asymmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: In the asymmetric complex, each protein monomer binds two different half DNA molecules.
source: Each protein monomer binds two different half DNA molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the asymmetric complex, the topoisomerase domain remains blocked by the (HhH)2 domains preventing access to the active site.
source: The topoisomerase domain remains blocked by the (HhH)2 domains preventing access to the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the asymmetric complex, one DNA is surrounded by the (HhH)2 domains while the other sits between (HhH)2 domains.
source: In this structure, one DNA is surrounded by the (HhH)2 domains while the other sits between (HhH)2 domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The seventh repeat forms an (HhH)2 domain followed by a long helix (Linker helix II) that connects it to the eighth (HhH)2 domain.
source: In the complex structure this region is ordered in one of the monomers and shows that the seventh repeat forms an (HhH)2 domain followed by a long helix (Linker helix II) that connects it to the eighth (HhH)2 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Linker helix II sits in the major groove of one DNA molecule, making the (HhH)2 domains wrap around the DNA.
source: This long helix sits in the major groove of one DNA molecule, making the (HhH)2 domains wrap around the DNA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the closed conformation the main change in the protein structure is the movement of (HhH)2 repeats 8–10 to enclose the DNA and the ordering of the seventh domain and the linker region.
source: Thus, in the closed conformation the main change in the protein structure is the movement of (HhH)2 repeats 8–10 to enclose the DNA and the ordering of the seventh domain and the linker region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the asymmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The same DNA sequence without the abasic site also crystallized under the same conditions, suggesting that the presence of the DNA abasic site had no effect on the binding of the protein or the conformation of the DNA.
source: Interestingly, the same DNA sequence without the abasic site also crystallized under the same conditions, suggesting that the presence of the DNA abasic site had no effect on the binding of the protein or the conformation of the DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the asymmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The structure of the symmetric oligonucleotide complex shows that each DNA fragment binds two protein molecules with the topoisomerase active site accessible and occupied by DNA.
source: The structure of the symmetric oligonucleotide complex shows that each DNA fragment binds two protein molecules with the topoisomerase active site accessible and occupied by DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the symmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The two monomers in the symmetric complex are related by a twofold axis, but this axis does not coincide with the DNA sequence twofold axis creating an asymmetry in the DNA structure.
source: The two monomers are related by a twofold axis, but this axis does not coincide with the DNA sequence twofold axis creating an asymmetry in the DNA structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the symmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: The two protein monomers in the symmetric complex are very similar in conformation and are related by an almost perfect noncrystallographic twofold axis (rmsd between Cα ~ 1.0 Å).
source: The two proteins in the asymmetric unit are very similar in conformation and are related by an almost perfect noncrystallographic twofold axis (rmsd between Cα ~ 1.0 Å).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the symmetric DNA complex structure.

claim: Each (HhH)2 domains subset has the same conformation as observed in the DNA-free protein, showing that they move as rigid groups.
source: Each (HhH)2 domains subset has the same conformation as observed in the DNA-free protein (Rajan et al., 2016), showing that they move as rigid groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison with a previous structure (Rajan et al., 2016).

claim: The topoisomerase domain is shifted with respect to the (HhH)2 domains and is accessible to the DNA in the symmetric complex.
source: The topoisomerase domain is shifted with respect to the (HhH)2 domains and is accessible to the DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The topoisomerase domain moves as a rigid body with the only changes observed confined to the helix linking the topoisomerase domain and the first (HhH)2 domain (Linker helix I).
source: The topoisomerase domain moves as a rigid body with the only changes observed confined to the helix linking the topoisomerase domain and the first (HhH)2 domain (Linker helix I) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Linker helix I is broken and separates the topoisomerase domain from the (HhH)2 domains by rotating the topoisomerase domain by close to 180°.
source: This helix, which in the DNA-free structure is an extension of the first helix of the (HhH)2 domain, is broken and in this way separates the topoisomerase domain from the (HhH)2 domains by rotating the topoisomerase domain by close to 180°. (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The surface area at the interface between the topoisomerase domain and the (HhH)2 domains is reduced considerably once the domains separate, suggesting that the closed form is more stable in the absence of DNA/protein interactions.
source: The surface area at the interface between the topoisomerase domain and the (HhH)2 domains is reduced considerably once the domains separate (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the closed form is more stable in the absence of DNA/protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The suggestion is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: In both conformations the residues at the interface are mostly hydrophilic amino acids, which is consistent with amino acids that can be either buried or exposed in the two conformations.
source: Interestingly, in both conformations the residues at the interface are mostly hydrophilic amino acids, which is consistent with amino acids that can be either buried or exposed in the two conformations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the structure.

claim: The change in Linker helix I is the only major change observed when the DNA-free and DNA-bound structures are compared.
source: The change in this helix is the only major change observed when the DNA-free and DNA-bound structures are compared.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: The movement of the topoisomerase domain exposes the active site and allows the end of the DNA molecule to enter the topoisomerase domain and interact with residues near the active site region.
source: The movement of the topoisomerase domain exposes the active site (Figure 2), which in all other structures was inaccessible, and allows the end of the DNA molecule to enter the topoisomerase domain and interacts with residues near the active site region (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The abasic site is accommodated by unstacking the complementary base, which moves to lie in the major groove of the DNA.
source: The structure shows that the abasic site is accommodated by unstacking the complementary base, which moves to lie in the major groove of the DNA (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The sugar of the abasic site remains in the expected position.
source: The sugar of the abasic site remains in the expected position.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DNA structure.

claim: The base adjacent to the abasic site moves to occupy the vacant space left by the abasic site.
source: The result of the rearrangements is that the base adjacent to the abasic site moves to occupy the vacant space left by the abasic site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DNA structure.

claim: The rearrangements around the abasic site create a kink in the DNA leading to an opening of the major groove and a narrowing of the major groove just before the abasic site.
source: These movements creates a kink in the DNA leading to an opening of the major groove and a narrowing of the major groove just before the abasic site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DNA structure.

claim: The bending around the abasic site allows the DNA to approach the active site.
source: The bending around the abasic site allows the DNA to approach the active site (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The DNA is very sharply bent where it enters the active site.
source: In addition, in order to interact with the protein the DNA is very sharply bent where it enters the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The sharp bend makes the two DNA strands melt and the last two complementary nucleotides are not base paired (T1:A39,G2:C38).
source: This sharp bend makes the two DNA strands melt and the last two complementary nucleotides are not base paired (T1:A39,G2:C38) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: C38 is unstacked and enters the minor groove, whereas A39 stacks on top of G37.
source: Instead, C38 is unstacked and enters the minor groove, whereas A39 stacks on top of G37 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The melting allows the last four nucleotides on the 3′ end of the DNA to enter the protein and do not interact with the other DNA strand.
source: The melting allows the last four nucleotides on the 3′ end of the DNA to enter the protein and do not interact with the other DNA strand (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 5′ end of the DNA has two unpaired nucleotides, the first one mostly disordered as it has moved away from the protein whereas the second nucleotide, G2, enters a pocket in the protein, stacked against the side chains of Tyr289 and Arg109.
source: The 5′ end of the DNA has two unpaired nucleotides, the first one mostly disordered as it has moved away from the protein whereas the second nucleotide, G2, enters a pocket in the protein, stacked against the side chains of Tyr289 and Arg109.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DNA structure.

claim: The (HhH)2 domains form a loop with a positively charged interior that accommodated the DNA.
source: They form a loop with a positively charged interior that accommodated the DNA, but appears to have few close contacts (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There are no contacts of the (HhH)2 domains with the bases, only with the backbone.
source: There are no contacts of the (HhH)2 domains with the bases, only with the backbone, which is not unusual for a nonsequence-specific DNA-binding protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA-protein interactions.

claim: Repeats 3–6 and 9 make contacts with the phosphate backbone while the rest of the repeats only surround it, but do not come close to it.
source: Repeats 3–6 and 9 make contacts with the phosphate backbone while the rest of the repeats only surround it, but do not come close to it.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA-protein interactions.

claim: Even though many of the repeats do not contact the DNA directly, they have positively charged residues facing the DNA, creating an overall positively charged environment around the DNA.
source: Interestingly, even though many of the repeats do not contact the DNA directly, they have positively charged residues facing the DNA, creating an overall positively charged environment around the DNA (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The abasic sites are not in direct contact with the protein even though the abasic sites were introduced as a possible target for the single intact repair domain.
source: The abasic sites are not in direct contact with the protein even though the abasic sites were introduced as a possible target for the single intact repair domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA-protein interactions.

claim: Repeat 6 contains an AP/dRP lyase active site that includes lysines 566, 570, and 571.
source: Repeat 6 contains an AP/dRP lyase active site that includes lysines 566, 570, and 571; mutations of any of these three residues are deleterious for activity (Rajan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to Rajan et al., 2013.

claim: In the complex structure, lysines 570 and 571 face the DNA phosphate backbone, but are not close enough to contact it.
source: In the complex structure, lysines 570 and 571 face the DNA phosphate backbone, but are not close enough to contact it.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA-protein interactions.

claim: Lysine 566 faces away from the DNA and cannot contact the DNA, suggesting that either lysine 570 or 571 are the likely nucleophile.
source: Lysine 566 faces away from the DNA and cannot contact the DNA, suggesting that either lysine 570 or 571 are the likely nucleophile.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural observation.

claim: It is likely that the protein scans the DNA for lesions by sliding along the DNA.
source: It is likely that the protein scans the DNA for lesions by sliding along the DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: The active site is exposed in the structure and reveals a highly positively charge region where the DNA enters.
source: The active site is exposed in the structure and reveals a highly positively charge region where the DNA enters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Binding of DNA in the active site region is plastic, with oligonucleotides of different lengths accommodated by following a slightly different path before entering the active site.
source: Binding of DNA in this region is plastic. Oligonucleotides of different lengths can be accommodated by following a slightly different path before entering the active site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 5′ end of one strand always follows the same path whereas the 3′ end does not.
source: The 5′ end of one strand always follows the same path whereas the 3′ end does not.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA binding.

claim: The contacts between the protein and the DNA are mostly with the phosphate backbone, with the bases facing the solvent.
source: The contacts between the protein and the DNA are mostly with the phosphate backbone, with the bases facing the solvent, although one nucleobase at the 5′ end is tightly wedged between two protein side chains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DNA-protein interactions.

claim: Arg37Ala showed reduced DNA relaxation activity.
source: Two of them showed noticeably reduced activity whereas three of them show wild-type levels of activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Lys134Ala showed reduced DNA relaxation activity.
source: Two of them showed noticeably reduced activity whereas three of them show wild-type levels of activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Lys47Ala, His56Ala, and Arg135Ala showed wild-type levels of DNA relaxation activity.
source: Two of them showed noticeably reduced activity whereas three of them show wild-type levels of activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: The double mutant Lys134Ala/Arg135Ala showed no DNA relaxation activity.
source: Interestingly, a double mutant with two positively charged residues mutated to alanine showed no activity, suggesting that while the enzyme can accommodate small charge changes, more extensive changes abolish the activity and confirming the importance of the positively charged region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Ala132Ile reduced very significantly the DNA relaxation activity, suggesting that the structure of this region is important for DNA binding.
source: Another mutant was designed to test the structure of a loop that abuts against the cleaved DNA strand; Ala132 faces the interior of the protein and replacing it with a bulkier isoleucine (Ala132Ile) reduced very significantly the activity, suggesting that the structure of this region is important for DNA binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Arg108Ala completely abolishes DNA relaxation activity, suggesting that Arg108 is an essential residue.
source: Arg108 lies between the two DNA strands and mutating it to alanine completely abolishes activity, suggesting that Arg108 is an essential residue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Arg83Ala and Arg109Ala resulted in reduced DNA relaxation activity with Arg83Ala showing a much lower level of activity.
source: Both Arg83 and Arg109 face the noncleaved strand and mutating them separately to alanine resulted in reduced relaxation activity with Arg83Ala showing a much lower level of activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Combining Arg108Ala and Arg109Ala completely abolishes DNA relaxation activity.
source: Combining Arg108Ala and Arg109Ala completely abolishes activity, which is not surprising as R108 is essential.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Mutating Arg288, Tyr289, and Arg293 to alanine had no effect on DNA relaxation activity.
source: Mutating Arg288, Tyr289, and Arg293 to alanine had no effect on activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Leu290Pro abolished DNA relaxation activity almost completely.
source: Finally, mutating Leu290 to proline abolishes activity almost completely.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: The Arg288Glu/Leu290Pro/Arg293Glu triple mutant has no DNA relaxation activity.
source: Not surprising, an Arg288Glu/Leu290Pro/Arg293Glu triple mutant has no activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: The ability of the linker helix to change conformation has the most dramatic effect on DNA relaxation activity.
source: The results show that while amino acids that approach the DNA are important, the ability of the linker helix to change conformation has the most dramatic effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Aside from Tyr226, five residues were identified as playing a role in the cleavage/religation reaction: Arg131, Arg144, His200, Glu215, and Lys218.
source: Aside from Tyr226, the active site tyrosine, five residues were identified as playing a role in the cleavage/religation reaction: Arg131, Arg144, His200, Glu215, and Lys218.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work (Taneja et al., 2006; Rajan et al., 2014).

claim: Aside from Lys218 all active site residues are in the vicinity of the DNA in the complex structure.
